subject: Platform business model
excerpt: I’ve been thinking about platform business model a lot this weekend…if we make it so devs can generate revenue for us in different ways, then it makes it more acceptable for us to charge them quite a bit more for using platform. The basic idea is that any other revenue you generate for us earns you a credit towards whatever fees you own us for using plaform. For most developers this would probably cover cost completely.
context: Facebook's CEO sketches charging developers for friends data, with credits for buying ads or using Facebook payments.

source.title: DCMS Committee: Note by the Chair and selected documents ordered from Six4Three, published 2018-12-05

subject: Platform revenue and data leaks
excerpt: I’m generally sceptical that there is as much data leak strategic risk as you think. I agree there is clear risk on the advertiser side, but I haven’t figured out how that connects to the rest of the platform. I think we leak info to developers, but I just can’t think if any instances where that data has leaked from developer to developer and caused a real issue for us.
context: Zuckerberg answers a colleague who argued for locking down friends data on Facebook's developer platform.

source.title: DCMS Committee: Note by the Chair and selected documents ordered from Six4Three, published 2018-12-05

subject: Platform revenue and data leaks
excerpt: Without limiting distribution or access to friends who use this app, I don’t think we have any way to get developers to pay us at all besides offering payments and ad networks.
context: In the same exchange Zuckerberg ties restricting friends data to getting developers to pay.

source.title: DCMS Committee: Note by the Chair and selected documents ordered from Six4Three, published 2018-12-05

subject: Data reciprocity
excerpt: We are going to require that all platform partners agree to data reciprocity. If you access a certain type of data (e.g. music listens), you must allow the user to publish back that same kind of data.
context: A Facebook platform executive announces the reciprocity rule for developers.

source.title: DCMS Committee: Note by the Chair and selected documents ordered from Six4Three, published 2018-12-05

subject: Platform business
excerpt: After thinking about platform business for a long time, I wanted to send out a note explaining where I’m leaning on this. This isn’t final and we’ll have a chance to discuss this in person before we decide this for sure, but since this is complex, I wanted to write out my thoughts. This is long, but hopefully helpful. The quick summary is that I think we should go with full reciprocity and access to app friends for no charge.
context: Zuckerberg sets out his preferred model for Facebook's 2012 platform changes.

source.title: DCMS Committee: Note by the Chair and selected documents ordered from Six4Three, published 2018-12-05

subject: Platform business
excerpt: However, that may be good for the world but it’s not good for us unless people also share back to Facebook and that content increases the value of our network. So ultimately, I think the purpose of platform – even the read side – is to increase sharing back into Facebook.
context: From the same note: Zuckerberg states what Facebook's developer platform is for.

source.title: DCMS Committee: Note by the Chair and selected documents ordered from Six4Three, published 2018-12-05

subject: Re: Platform business
excerpt: I like full reciprocity and this is the heart of why.
context: Facebook's COO replies to Zuckerberg's note on the platform business model.

Unless anyone raises objections, we will shut down their friends API access today. We’ve prepared reactive PR, and I will let Jana know our decision.

subject: Android permissions update
excerpt: They are going to include the ‘read call log’ permission, which will trigger the Android permissions dialog on update, requiring users to accept the update. They will then provide an in-app opt in NUX for a feature that lets you continuously upload your SMS and call log history to Facebook to be used for improving things like PYMK, coefficient calculation, feed ranking etc. This is a pretty high-risk thing to do from a PR perspective but it appears that the growth team will charge ahead and do it.
context: A Facebook product manager warns colleagues about the call log permission planned for the Android app.

subject: Android permissions update
excerpt: The Growth team is now exploring a path where we only request Read Call Log permission, and hold off on requesting any other permissions for now. Based on their initial testing, it seems this would allow us to upgrade users without subjecting them to an Android permissions dialog at all.
context: A Facebook privacy executive describes how the permission change could avoid showing users a dialog.

subject: Java alternatives

context: A Google engineer writes to the head of Android; the email was shown to the jury in Oracle v. Google.

subject: Buying the rights to Java
excerpt: Certainly a clever idea. I’ll ask our team to pursue.

source.title: Oracle v. Google, N.D. Cal. No. 3:10-cv-03561, Dkt 1168 (Oracle Rule 50(a) motion, 2012-05-16)

subject: Meeting with Google
excerpt: Tom and I spoke with Martin Buccholz today. I delivered the message that they have only two options: OpenJDK or Commercial Use, which would require compatibility. I also explained that using Java in the context of customer-facing applications is considered by Sun to be commercial use. I also explained that if they choose the commercial use/compatibility option, it would have ramifications throughout Google, and I gave Android as an example.
context: A Sun licensing manager reports telling Google it needed either OpenJDK or a compatible commercial license.

source.title: Oracle v. Google, N.D. Cal. No. 3:10-cv-03561, Dkt 1168 (Oracle Rule 50(a) motion, 2012-05-16)

subject: Sun meeting
excerpt: As expected, this does not look promising. Leo says Sun has an inflexible licensing model where Open JDK never gets any support of any kind, and the commercial version of the code does (and mostly Sun is thinking of support for binaries). Also, Sun would want any discussions with Google to involve other inter-company issues, in particular Android, which I’m sure we would want to keep separate. Android seems to be a big deal at Sun.
context: A Google engineer's internal report of the same meeting with Sun.

source.title: Oracle v. Google, N.D. Cal. No. 3:10-cv-03561, Dkt 1168 (Oracle Rule 50(a) motion, 2012-05-16)

subject: Re: Sun meeting
excerpt: Actually, having said that I wonder whether this is too close to dangerous territory, and with too little chance of anything positive coming of it for us to be messing around? We really don’t want to inadvertently stir anything up for Android, and Leo has said pretty clearly that they don’t have anything for us as regards security patches. I suspect we should step away, and only respond further if Sun chases after us.
context: A Google engineer, a former Sun employee, advises against more talks with Sun about Java.

subject: Re: iBookstore

All the major publishers tell us that Amazon’s $9.99 price for new releases is eroding the value perception of their products in customer’s minds, and they do not want this practice to continue for new releases. 3. source.title: United States v. Apple Inc., S.D.N.Y. No. 12 Civ. 2826 (DLC), Opinion & Order, Dkt 326, 2013-07-10

subject: Re: iBookstore
excerpt: The current business model of companies like Amazon distributing ebooks below cost or without making a reasonable profit isn’t sustainable for long. As ebooks become a larger business, distributors will need to make at least a small profit, and you will want this too so that they invest in the future of the business with infrastructure, marketing, etc.
context: The first of six points in Jobs's long reply to the HarperCollins parent's concerns.

source.title: United States v. Apple Inc., S.D.N.Y. No. 12 Civ. 2826 (DLC), Opinion & Order, Dkt 326, 2013-07-10

subject: Re: iBookstore
excerpt: Heck, Amazon is selling these books at $9.99, and who knows, maybe they are right and we will fail even at $12.99. But we’re willing to try at the prices we’ve proposed. We are not willing to try at higher prices because we are pretty sure we’ll all fail.
context: Jobs on Apple's e-book price caps; Apple's lawyers cited the "maybe they are right" line at trial.

source.title: United States v. Apple Inc., S.D.N.Y. No. 12 Civ. 2826 (DLC), Opinion & Order, Dkt 326, 2013-07-10

subject: Re: iBookstore
excerpt: As I see it, HC has the following choices: 1. Throw in with apple and see if we can all make a go of this to create a real mainstream ebooks market at $12.99 and $14.99. 2. Keep going with Amazon at $9.99. You will make a bit more money in the short term, but in the medium term Amazon will tell you they will be paying you 70% of $9.99. They have shareholders too.
context: Jobs lays out HarperCollins's options three days before the iPad launch.

source.title: United States v. Apple Inc., S.D.N.Y. No. 12 Civ. 2826 (DLC), Opinion & Order, Dkt 326, 2013-07-10

subject: Re: iBookstore
excerpt: Hold back your books from Amazon. Without a way for customers to buy your ebooks, they will steal them. This will be the start of piracy and once started there will be no stopping it. Trust me, I’ve seen this happen with my own eyes. Maybe I’m missing something, but I don’t see any other alternatives. Do you?
context: The third option in Jobs's email to Murdoch, and his closing question.
